newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FLI signs Camp John Hay lease agreement.
newsitem.headline: FLI signs Camp John Hay lease agreement.

text.p: The Philippine government's Bases Conversion Development Authority (Basecon) said on Saturday it had signed a 25-year lease agreement with Fil-Estate and Penta Capital for the development of Camp John Hay.

"The agreement is now a done deal. The Fil-Estate Penta Capital group submitted a $100 million bid bond to ensure the development of John Hay," Basecon spokesman Ed Javier said by telephone from the northern Philippine hill resort of Baguio.

Javier said the group had also submitted another 250 million pesos as an advance payment on its 425 million peso rental for the first five years of the contract. The rental will be after this five-year period.

Basecon initially awarded the contract to manage and develop a 270 hectare property inside the former U.S. military base in Baguio to a Filipino-Thai group, Manuela Land and Homes, but it failed to meet a deadline for signing the contract.

Manuela, made up of Philippine shopping mall owner Manuela Corp and Thai property firm Land and Houses Plc, submitted a bid of 1.588 billion pesos for the contract, about four times as much as the second-placed bidder, the Fil-Estate Penta group.
Manuela later said it had been misled over the amount of land available for development.
Javier said the Basecon planned to turn over management of Camp John Hay to the Fil-Estate group at the "earliest possible time".
"The Fil-Estate group said they planned to improve the existing facilities in Camp John Hay, but they will ensure that environmental safeguards are met," Javier added.

The Fil-Estate consortium is composed of Fil-Estate Land Inc and its affiliate Fil-Estate Management Inc, with 25 percent, and College Assurance Plans Philippines Inc, with another 25 percent equity, and Penta Capital Holdings Inc, Ramcar Inc, La Paz Homes Cavite Development Corp, and Philodrill Corp, with 10 percent each.
The government's first attempt to privatise John Hay in 1994 failed after a consortium led by Taiwan's Tuntex Corp, bailed out after local protests over the environmental impact of the development.
